name: Sidamo
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Kawachi, Kazuhiro. 2007. A grammar of Sidaama (Sidamo), a Cushitic language of Ethiopia. SUNY Buffalo dissertation (ProQuest, paywalled); also Anbessa Teferra 2014 Sidaama grammar.

new_statements.quote: In all five HEC languages there appears to be a general rule of stress on word-final long vowels and (rarely) diphthongs, and stress on the vowel of the next-to-last syllable when there is no word-final long vowel or diphthong. I have not indicated stress which is consistent with this rule (including in words from Sasse 1982), but stress is marked where this general rule is violated, for example not uncommonly on word-final short vowels. It is possible that stressed word-final vowels are phonemically long; presumably they are historically so.
new_statements.citation: Hudson, Grover. 1989. Highland East Cushitic Dictionary (Kuschitische Sprachstudien / Cushitic Language Studies 7). Hamburg: Helmut Buske Verlag.
new_statements.locator: Introduction, section 'Word stress', p. 6 (scan PDF p. 14)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress goes on the final syllable if it contains a long vowel or diphthong; otherwise on the penultimate syllable. Deviations (stress on a final short vowel) are lexically marked and may reflect underlying/historical final length. Stated as a generalization over all five HEC languages including Sidamo, not for Sidamo alone.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'not uncommonly' on word-final short vowels, marked individually in the dictionary; author suspects such vowels are phonemically (historically) long. Older source Moreno 1940 (pp. 18-19, saved) says the accent is very unstable, shifts within the phrase, and cannot be reduced to rules. Kawachi (BLS 2007: 260 n. 2, saved) treats the system as pitch: accusative case is marked by high pitch on the stem-final vowel, i.e. accent is partly morphological.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; dictionary citation forms (nouns cited in the accusative, verbs as stems). Hedged ('there appears to be'). The modern primary description (Kawachi 2007 dissertation; Anbessa Teferra 2000/2014) describes Sidaama as a pitch-accent language and would supersede this.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted Hudson 1989 rule is stated for all five Highland East Cushitic languages jointly (Burji burj1245, Gedeo gede1246, Hadiyya hadi1240, Kambaata kamb1316, Sidamo sida1246), not for Sidamo specifically; Hudson's Sidamo data are from his own fieldwork (dictionary based on Sidamo, Gedeo, Hadiyya, Kambata plus Sasse's Burji). Modern work (Kawachi 2007 and later) treats Sidaama as a pitch-accent language in which some high pitches are morphological (e.g. accusative = high pitch on stem-final vowel), so 'stress' here should be read as pitch accent. Moreno 1940 describes the northern Sidamo of the Italian-era Sidamo Commissariat (same language, older data).

sources.note: Accent in Sidamo, as in other Cushitic languages and Amharic, is 'molto incostante', shifting position within the phrase for psychological reasons and rhythmic combinations, with tendencies like those he described for Galla (Oromo) but not reducible to rules at the present state of knowledge; marked in the grammar where observed to prevail, mostly not marked in the lexicon. Also: accented vowels tend to lengthen, unaccented to shorten; long accented vowels written with circumflex (p. 18); a stressed vowel immediately before an enclitic/suffix geminates its consonant (p. 21).

sources.citation: Appleyard, David L. 1991. The role of tone in some Cushitic languages. York Papers in Linguistics 15: 5-32 (ERIC ED338062).
sources.note: Secondary/comparative: quotes Bender (ed.) 1976 p. 248 that 'Stress is phonemic in at least four of the [HEC] languages' (attributed to 'Gragg 1976' but Gragg's chapter is pp. 166-195 per Appleyard's own bibliography, so p. 248 is inside G. Hudson's HEC chapter); gives Sidamo minimal pairs for accent (e.g. t'aTmi 'he asked' vs. imperative; ango 'he has drunk' vs. 'let us drink'); says tone/accent plays some part in morphological marking in Sidamo.
